one_liner: Julia 1.9 Base sort! (LSD radix sort on Float64 bit patterns) timed against std::sort and qsort built at -O0; not a valid C++ comparison.
what_it_does: An 11-star benchmark repo (no license, last commit 2023-02-17) by the author of Julia 1.9's sorting rewrite. Each language fills a vector of 3^i uniform random Float64 values, sorts it with that language's default sort, takes a dot product with 1..n, and subtracts a no-sort control run to estimate sort time in ns per element; data.txt holds one trial per size on a 2019 MacBook Air (1.6 GHz dual-core i5). The thing being catalogued is plain Base.sort!(v::Vector{Float64}) in Julia 1.9 or later: no package, same call as before, in place.
how_it_is_fast: From Julia 1.9 the default sort for Float64 is no longer a comparison sort: IEEEFloatOptimization moves NaNs to the end, splits by sign and reinterprets the values as UInt64, then ConsiderRadixSort picks a stable least-significant-digit RadixSort when bits+70 < 22*log(n), after subtracting the minimum so fewer bits are radixed (base/sort.jl, v1.9.0-beta3 and still on master). For uniform [0,1) data that switch happens from about 3^6 = 729 elements; at 3^14 the range spans 57 bits, sorted in 6 counting passes of 10 bits with an n-element scratch buffer. Julia 1.8.5 still used an unstable QuickSort with integer comparisons, which is why its 92.5 ns per element at 3^14 trails Rust's optimized pdqsort-based sort_unstable_by (68.5 ns) in the same table.
when_to_use: You are already in Julia and sort large plain vectors of Float64, Float32 or machine integers (thousands to tens of millions of elements): default sort! picks radix sort with no code change; 35.1 ns per element at 4.78M doubles on a 1.6 GHz i5 in this run.

As a hint for C++ work: a sort-bound step on large float or integer keys gains more from an LSD radix sort over the uint-mapped bit pattern than from tuning a comparison sort; on the same laptop Julia 1.9's radix sort was about 1.95x faster than Rust's release-built sort_unstable_by (35.1 vs 68.5 ns per element, derived from page data).

When NaNs may appear: Julia's default sort! is defined for every Float64 (NaNs go to the end), while std::sort with operator< on data containing NaN violates strict weak ordering (undefined behaviour, the repo's issue #9).
As a starting harness for a fair re-run: the generate, sort, dot-product, subtract-control design is easy to port; fix the C and C++ build lines first.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Julia beats optimized C++ std::sort: the C and C++ rows were built with 'gcc script.c' and 'g++ -std=c++11 script.cpp' (Apple clang 13, no -O flag, so -O0; plot.jl confirms the commands), while Rust used --release, so the 5.9x (Julia 1.9) and 2.2x (Julia 1.8) leads over C++ are mostly a build artifact.

As a comparison-sort result: the gap is algorithmic (radix sort against introsort and qsort); the open issue #11 objects to exactly this reading, and the author replies that the repo only gives 'a rough idea of performance across languages'.
For sorts with a custom lt, a by key, structs or strings: those inputs are not UIntMappable and fall back to ScratchQuickSort, so nothing here applies.
When memory is tight: the radix path allocates an n-element scratch buffer (plus a 2^chunk_size count array) where std::sort is in place.
Below a few hundred elements: radix sort is not chosen and the per-element numbers at 3^1 to 3^5 are dominated by noise and JIT effects (Julia 1.9 row 1 is 145.2 ns, including compilation).

integration.form: module (Julia Base; the benchmark repo itself is a set of standalone scripts)
integration.dependencies: none (Julia standard library Random for the benchmark's rand!)
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 1.9 for the radix-sort default (measured on 1.9.0-beta3); Julia 1.8.5 uses QuickSort
integration.platforms: any platform Julia supports; measured only on an x86-64 macOS laptop
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded; sort! mutates its argument in place, so concurrent calls need distinct vectors (not documented beyond that)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same role as std::sort for Julia code, but nothing callable from C++ without embedding Julia or porting base/sort.jl's RadixSort

gotchas: Crippled baseline: C and C++ were compiled at -O0 (no -O flag on Apple clang 13), while Rust ran cargo --release; the C++ figure is also not a sort time: script.cpp prints total runtime (allocation, generation, sort, dot product) times a fixed 0.85 because the author saw negative differences ('strange bug', issue #1), and it stops at 3^14 while other languages run to 3^15.

script.cpp allocates a fresh std::vector<double>(n) and constructs a default-seeded std::default_random_engine for every repetition, so every repetition of one size sorts identical data and pays allocation and zero-fill inside the timed region; the C row times qsort through a function-pointer comparator compiled at -O0.

Each data point is a single trial (README), on a dual-core laptop; the owner later said a reporter on a Xeon Gold 6254 measured Julia about 4x slower relative to clock than on her machine and guessed at slower memory bandwidth (issue #1), so radix-sort gains depend on cache and memory behaviour.
No LICENSE file in the benchmark repo, so its scripts are reference only; Julia Base itself is MIT.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this only to learn which algorithm Julia's default Float64 sort uses and roughly how fast it is; for a Julia-versus-C++ sort measurement with optimized C++ builds the LangArena Sort::Self sibling (Julia 1.13 against std::sort at -O2 and -O3) is the better-evidenced entry, and the radix-versus-comparison confound applies there too.
verified_claims_summary: On a 2019 MacBook Air (1.6 GHz dual-core i5), one trial per size, sorting 3^14 = 4,782,969 uniform Float64 values took 35.1 ns per element with Julia 1.9.0-beta3 (radix sort) and 92.5 with Julia 1.8.5 (QuickSort), against 207.6 for C++ std::sort and 307.2 for C qsort, both built by Apple clang 13 at -O0; Rust 1.67 sort_unstable_by at --release took 68.5 and glidesort 79.4. Only the Rust row is an optimized native comparison, and Julia 1.9 beats it by about 1.95x (derived from page data).
status_note: Abandoned benchmark (last commit 2023-02-17, open issues on NaN undefined behaviour in the C++ script and on comparison-sort fairness, no license) kept as reference at tier D; the radix-sort default it showcases ships in every Julia release since 1.9 and is still the dispatch in base/sort.jl on master.
